inputs.need:
I am a physiotherapist and clinical lead for musculoskeletal outpatients at a regional hospital that serves a large rural area. People with knee osteoarthritis wait about five months for a first appointment, and many live more than an hour's drive away. Since March we have run a six-week group exercise programme by video link: two 45-minute sessions a week with a physiotherapist, up to eight people per group, using the same exercise and education content as our in-person class. So far 64 people have started it and 49 finished all six weeks.

We would like to do a mixed-methods evaluation before the hospital decides whether to keep it and whether to offer it instead of the in-person class for some patients. For the numbers side, we routinely collect the KOOS-12 knee score, the 30-second chair stand test (done at home with a chair and a video call) and attendance, before and after the programme and at three months. For the experience side, we want to understand who finds video sessions workable and who does not, especially older people, people with poor internet or little computer confidence, and people whose first language is not English. Some patients told us the video class was the only way they could attend at all, while others dropped out after the first week because of connection problems.

I need help with a clear main question, which quantitative outcome should be primary, how many people we need, how to sample for interviews so we hear from people who stopped attending, and how to bring the two strands together at the end. We have no funding beyond staff time, and the programme cannot be withheld from anyone who wants it.
inputs.constraints: No funding beyond staff time. The video programme cannot be withheld from anyone who wants it. Interviews must be done by a physiotherapist who does not run the participant's own group. Data collection must finish by June 2027.

records.title: Physiotherapist-led exercise by video versus in person for knee osteoarthritis: a randomised non-inferiority comparison
records.authors: Lindahl-Mwangi C, Okafor-Stein R, Brennan-Tran H
records.abstract: Background: exercise therapy is first-line care for knee osteoarthritis, but attendance at hospital classes is limited by travel. Methods: we randomly allocated 175 adults with knee osteoarthritis to six weeks of physiotherapist-led group exercise by video or the same programme in person, with a non-inferiority margin of 8 points on the KOOS pain subscale. Results: at 12 weeks the mean difference in KOOS pain change was 1.4 points in favour of in-person exercise (95 percent CI -2.9 to 5.7), within the margin. Session attendance was 78 percent by video and 81 percent in person. Satisfaction scores were similar. Participants were recruited from urban clinics and needed their own device. Conclusions: video delivery was non-inferior for pain at 12 weeks in people who could use the technology.

records.title: Telehealth-delivered exercise therapy for knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised comparisons
records.authors: Petrov-Achebe N, Sandoval-Reid J, Kamau-Lindgren T
records.abstract: We searched five databases to June 2022 for randomised comparisons of exercise therapy delivered by telehealth for knee osteoarthritis. In total, 14 trials with 1,720 participants were included. Compared with in-person exercise, telehealth-delivered exercise showed no important difference in pain (standardised mean difference 0.05, 95 percent CI -0.10 to 0.20) or in physical function. Compared with no exercise, telehealth exercise improved pain and function. Heterogeneity was moderate. Most trials excluded people without internet access, and adults over 75 and people with low digital literacy were under-represented, which limits applicability to rural and older populations. Certainty was rated moderate for pain and low for function.

records.title: Older adults' experiences of group exercise classes delivered by video: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 19 adults aged 65 to 86 who had taken part in physiotherapy group exercise classes by video. Participants valued not having to travel or arrange transport and said they exercised more regularly at home. Frustration with technology was common in the first sessions, and several said a practice call before the first class would have helped. Some missed the social contact of an in-person class and found it harder to ask questions in a video group. Participants who lived alone relied on family members to set up the device. The authors recommend a technology check before the first session and small groups that allow questions.

records.title: Attendance and completion in a rural telehealth knee exercise programme: a service cohort
records.authors: Ferreira-Oyelaran L, McAllister-Dube K, Suzuki-Hale P
records.abstract: We describe 212 people with knee osteoarthritis who started a six-week video exercise programme run by a rural hospital physiotherapy service. Overall, 71 percent completed the programme. Completion was 52 percent among participants without home broadband and 76 percent among those with it, and 60 percent among participants aged over 75 compared with 74 percent among younger participants. Among completers, the mean KOOS-12 summary score improved by 9.8 points at six weeks. Outcomes were not recorded for people who stopped attending, and there was no comparison group, so the improvement cannot be attributed to the programme alone.

records.title: Reliability of the 30-second chair stand test performed by video call in people with knee osteoarthritis
records.abstract: We compared the 30-second chair stand test performed at home by video call with the same test performed in clinic on the same day in 48 people with knee osteoarthritis. Agreement was high (intraclass correlation 0.91), and the mean difference was 0.4 stands, with more stands counted in clinic. Two participants could not position the camera to show the whole movement, and one test was stopped because the chair was unstable. The authors recommend a standard chair height, a camera check and a second observer for the first remote test.

records.title: Digital exclusion and exercise therapy: who declines video-based physiotherapy and why
records.authors: Obi-Castellano R, Wainwright-Adeyemi J, Lund-Takahashi M
records.abstract: We invited 340 people referred for knee or hip exercise therapy to choose video-based or in-person physiotherapy and interviewed a purposive sample of those who declined video. Of the 340 people invited, 29 percent declined video-based physiotherapy. Declining was more common among people with limited English (46 percent) and among those without a smartphone. Interviews described fear of not coping with the technology, lack of a private space at home, and worry about being seen exercising by others in the group. Loaned devices and a telephone setup call were described as helpful by those who accepted after initially declining.

records.title: Travel distance and attendance at hospital physiotherapy for knee osteoarthritis in a rural region
records.abstract: We examined attendance records of 406 patients with knee osteoarthritis referred to hospital physiotherapy in a rural region. The median one-way travel distance was 68 km. Attendance was 83 percent of booked sessions among patients living within 20 km and 61 percent among those living more than 60 km away. Patients without a car and those relying on community transport attended least. Distance was also associated with longer waits for a first appointment. The authors suggest that services for dispersed rural populations consider remote delivery for exercise-based care.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A randomised non-inferiority comparison and a review of 14 trials find video or telehealth exercise about as effective for pain as in-person exercise in people who can use the technology. Applicability to the local population is the weak point: the trials under-represent older and digitally excluded people, a rural service reported lower completion without broadband and over age 75, and a mixed-methods study found that people with limited English more often declined video. Interview studies point to early technology problems and fewer chances to ask questions. The remote chair stand test agrees well with clinic testing. The evidence supports a local evaluation that measures outcomes for everyone who starts and explains who does not complete.
response.gradeRationale: Randomised and pooled evidence for similar pain outcomes, downgraded for indirectness to rural, older and digitally excluded users; access findings are low certainty from service data and qualitative studies.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims; overall certainty moderate.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven retrieved records (S13). Certainty is the appraisal's value over inspected records (G1).

response.reading: Travel is the main barrier to in-person classes, and video delivery removes it for people with a device, a connection and confidence. Trials show similar pain outcomes, but they mostly excluded the people the service worries about. Completion and uptake depend on broadband, age and language, so the programme could help most people while leaving a digitally excluded group behind. The quantitative strand tells the service whether outcomes are in the expected range; the qualitative strand explains who stops and why.

response.finer: Feasible within staff time and routine data; interesting to the hospital's decision in 2027; novel for a rural and older population; ethical with approved interviews; relevant because it decides whether video can replace some in-person classes.
response.summary: One quantitative and one qualitative question for a convergent design.

response.rationale: Two questions of different kinds must be answered together: whether outcomes among all starters are in the expected range (quantitative, routine data) and why some people cannot use video (qualitative, interviews). A convergent mixed-methods design collects both over the same period and integrates them in a joint display that places completion and outcome by subgroup next to interview themes. The retrieved evidence settles the effectiveness of the format (c1, c2) and points to unequal completion and uptake (c3, c4) that interviews must explain.

response.overview: Convergent mixed-methods evaluation of a six-week video group exercise programme: a quantitative strand using routine outcomes for every starter and a qualitative strand of semi-structured interviews, integrated at analysis in a joint display.
response.population: Adults with knee osteoarthritis who start the video programme between March 2026 and March 2027 (about 110 expected); interview participants sampled from starters and non-completers.
response.exposure: Six weeks of physiotherapist-led video group exercise, two 45-minute sessions a week, up to eight participants, with a technology check and loaned tablets where needed.
response.procedures: KOOS-12 and the remote chair stand test at baseline, six weeks and three months; non-completers are telephoned at three months for KOOS-12. Interviews of 30 to 45 minutes by a physiotherapist who did not run the participant's group, by telephone or video, with interpreters where needed. Sampling targets people over 75, people without home broadband, people with limited English and non-completers.

response.designSummary: Single-group before-and-after quantitative strand with all starters, and a qualitative strand analysed thematically; integration by joint display.
response.sampleSize: About 110 starters are expected by March 2027 and about 90 with a three-month score. With a standard deviation of change of about 16 points, 90 participants give a 95 percent confidence interval of about 3.3 points either side of the mean change, enough to tell whether the mean improvement is near the 8-point threshold in h1. For the interviews, 16 to 20 participants are planned, stopping when new interviews add no new barrier themes within each sampling group.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mean change in KOOS-12 summary score from baseline to three months with a 95 percent confidence interval among all starters, using multiple imputation for missing three-month scores and a complete-case analysis alongside.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Chair stand change; completion by age group, internet access and language with 95 percent intervals; reflexive thematic analysis of interviews by two analysts; a joint display comparing completion and outcome by subgroup with interview themes.
response.missingData: Three-month scores are sought by telephone from non-completers; the remaining missing scores are imputed using baseline score, age and attendance, with 20 imputations, and the number imputed is reported.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; subgroup completion rates are descriptive.

response.risks: Minimal: questionnaires and a home chair stand test already used in care, and interviews about experience. Risk of falls during home testing is managed by the camera check and a stable chair.
response.consent: Written or recorded verbal consent for interviews and for use of routine outcomes in the evaluation; declining does not affect access to either programme.
response.data: Routine outcomes extracted with a study number; interview recordings transcribed and deleted after checking; data kept on the hospital research drive for seven years.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: age, rurality, income, language and digital access shape who can use video. Interpreters, loaned tablets and telephone interviews are offered, and completion and outcomes are reported by age group, internet access and language.
response.effectiveness: The evaluation succeeds if it tells the hospital whether outcomes are in the expected range and which groups need an alternative to video.
response.efficiency: Uses routine data and 3 hours per week of staff time.
response.costs: Staff time and interpreter bookings within the service budget; four loaned tablets already owned.
response.grants: None needed; findings could support a regional application for digital inclusion support.
response.partnerships: Two patient partners with knee osteoarthritis, one of whom stopped the video programme, the hospital interpreting service and the regional library digital skills scheme.
response.rebPath: Approved by the research ethics board on 2026-09-19 (REB-26-0875) under TCPS 2 principles for the interview component; routine outcome use covered by the same approval.

response.title: Video-delivered group exercise for knee osteoarthritis in a rural physiotherapy service: a convergent mixed-methods evaluation
response.abstract: Objective: to describe outcomes and experiences of a six-week video group exercise programme for knee osteoarthritis in a rural service. Design: convergent mixed-methods evaluation. Quantitative strand: KOOS-12 change at three months for all starters and completion by subgroup. Qualitative strand: 16 to 20 interviews including non-completers. Results and conclusions will follow data collection.
response.introduction: Video-delivered exercise gives similar pain outcomes to in-person exercise in trials, but trial participants were younger and digitally connected. Rural services need to know whether their own participants benefit and who is left out.
response.methods: All starters from March 2026 to March 2027 contribute routine outcomes, with telephone follow-up of non-completers. Interviews are sampled for age, internet access, language and completion. Results are integrated in a joint display.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present KOOS-12 change, completion by subgroup, interview themes and the joint display.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare local outcomes with the trial evidence and set out which groups need an in-person or supported alternative.
response.limitations: Single group without comparison; missing outcomes for some non-completers; one service.
response.reportingChecklist: GRAMMS with COREQ for the interview strand

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am a physiotherapist and clinical lead for musculoskeletal outpatients at a regional hospital that serves a large rural area. People with knee osteoarthritis wait about five months for a first appointment, and many live more than an hour's drive away. Since March we have run a six-week group exercise programme by video link: two 45-minute sessions a week with a physiotherapist, up to eight people per group, using the same exercise and education content as our in-person class. So far 64 people have started it and 49 finished all six weeks.

We would like to do a mixed-methods evaluation before the hospital decides whether to keep it and whether to offer it instead of the in-person class for some patients. For the numbers side, we routinely collect the KOOS-12 knee score, the 30-second chair stand test (done at home with a chair and a video call) and attendance, before and after the programme and at three months. For the experience side, we want to understand who finds video sessions workable and who does not, especially older people, people with poor internet or little computer confidence, and people whose first language is not English. Some patients told us the video class was the only way they could attend at all, while others dropped out after the first week because of connection problems.

I need help with a clear main question, which quantitative outcome should be primary, how many people we need, how to sample for interviews so we hear from people who stopped attending, and how to bring the two strands together at the end. We have no funding beyond staff time, and the programme cannot be withheld from anyone who wants it.
